title: Scalp acoustoelectric imaging needs about 40 minutes to 9 hours of neural activity per 1.6 mm focus to detect typical human cortical currents at FDA intensity, within about tenfold
abstract: Through the scalp, acoustoelectric imaging can at best detect typical human cortical currents in a few chosen voxels; it cannot map cortex in a practical time while the ultrasound stays inside diagnostic safety limits. This matters because groups propose transcranial acoustoelectric brain imaging as a noninvasive method with millimetre resolution. In this method, focused ultrasound changes tissue resistivity by a small fraction K·p (p is the pressure; K, the interaction constant, is 0.03–0.1 % per MPa in published work). Electrodes then record the brain's own current in the focus as a signal near the ultrasound frequency. We derived the signal from reciprocity and the noise from the thermal (Johnson) noise of the head. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) depends on the acoustic energy delivered during neural activity, not on the peak pressure. An electrode-free upper limit exists; scalp electrodes reach only 4e-7 to 1e-5 of it, because the skull separates them from the brain. We used a four-shell spherical head, typical evoked current (dipole moment density 0.25 nAm/mm²), a 1 MHz focus (1.6 mm by 11 mm), 0.72 W/cm² and K = 0.1 %/MPa. The best 475-electrode scalp array then needs about 40 minutes of neural activity for SNR 3 in a sulcal-wall voxel and about 9 hours at a gyral crown. With the ultrasound gated to a 0.1 s response per trial, this is 2,400 to 32,000 trials per voxel. Tissue conductivities at the 1 MHz carrier shorten these times 1.3–12 times; the measured K of tissue (0.04 %/MPa) lengthens them about 6 times. Epidural or subdural electrodes reduce the time to 3–30 s for cortex less than about 10 mm deep. Radio-frequency atomic magnetometers at 0.2 fT/√Hz would need about 1–2 minutes for sulcal-wall sources, but only with laboratory-grade sensors and strong suppression of the transducer's own field. Published papers cite evoked current densities up to 0.5 mA/cm²; physiological values are 0.006–0.08 mA/cm². In a 2026 mouse study, the published summary values imply sidebands 0.18 times the evoked potential; bulk acoustoelectric mixing allows 0.0005–0.002 for realistic foci and at most 0.07 in the most extreme geometry. The main limits are the spherical head, the unknown K and carrier-frequency conductivities of living tissue, and the use of summary statistics for the mouse comparison.

display.caption: Neural-activity time needed for SNR 3 in one voxel versus focus depth, for typical evoked activity (0.25 nAm/mm²), 1 MHz focus, 0.72 W/cm², K = 0.1 %/MPa and EEG-type conductivities (sheet approximation). Scalp arrays need about 1 hour or more; epidural, ECoG and RF-magnetometer readouts need seconds to minutes near the surface. Gray line: electrode-free thermal limit.
